name: Gareth Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Gareth. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm out of the Hollow Creek depot by half six, coffee in the flask, and the crew's usually four of us in two trucks. Most days it's rural overhead work: swapping rotten poles, restringing a span after a tree's come down on it, fixing a transformer that's taken a lightning hit. I like being up in the bucket on a clear morning with the fields all round you. What wears me out is storm call-outs, when you've done a full day and the phone goes at eleven at night and you're out till dawn in the rain.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been doing this, and who's at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Nineteen years with the company, apprenticeship straight out of school. My partner Mira's a nurse at the care home on Station Road, and we've got Ellie, who's twelve, and Sam, who's nine. We've got a mortgage on a semi with about fourteen years left on it, and maybe three months of money put by if things went wrong. I'm a union man, same as my dad was at the steelworks, and I'm not a gadget person. Mira does the online banking because I can't be bothered with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've been saying in the canteen for two years: told you so. Every few months some manager comes down from head office with a tablet and a new system, and six months later we're back to paper job sheets. You can't send an app up a pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it'd mean nothing changes for me, and that suits me fine. The office might get a few new screens, and maybe some of the clerks in billing lose hours, which I wouldn't be happy about. But for the crew it's the same poles, same storms, same pay deal every two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing. I'd go to the branch meetings like always and keep an eye on whether they use AI as an excuse to cut the office staff. Money-wise, nothing changes, we keep chipping at the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, if I'm honest. Like a forecast for a big storm that turns out to be a bit of drizzle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the billing clerks. Who are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a woman called Bev in the office at the depot who's done the call-out rosters for twenty years. If anyone loses out when they bring a computer in, it's people like Bev, not the managers who buy it. I'd want the union to stand up for her as much as for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ellie and Sam about AI in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them not to believe everything on their phones. Ellie's already asked me if robots will take my job, because some boy at school said so. In this picture I'd say, see, your dad's still climbing poles and the robots are still on TV.

S0.say: I've said all along it's mostly hype, and this proves it. They keep trying new systems on us and we always end up back on paper job sheets, because you can't send an app up a pole.
S0.think: It changes nothing for me and I'm glad of it. My only real worry is that the office staff, people like Bev on the rosters, lose hours while the managers who bought the systems keep their jobs.
S0.do: Carries on at the Hollow Creek depot as normal and keeps paying down the mortgage. Keeps going to union branch meetings and watches for AI being used as an excuse to cut office hours.
S0.feel: Relieved, like a storm warning that turns into drizzle.
S0.quote: Every few months some manager comes down from head office with a tablet and a new system, and six months later we're back to paper job sheets.
S0.fieldNote: Gareth sees the world through his union and his crew, and he measures new technology by whether it ever reached the bucket truck. His first concern in the calm picture was for an office worker, not himself. He takes some pride in never using these tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got to get it in writing. If they're bringing in drones to inspect lines or software to plan the jobs, fine, but the union needs a deal that says nobody gets laid off because of it. That's what I'd post in the members' group too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it worries me more than I'd let on. They've already trialled a drone on the long line out past Kettle Farm, and the guys joked it was coming for our jobs. If they do the inspection walks with drones and plan the crews with a computer, they need fewer of us, and I'm average at this, not the best.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push hard at the branch to get a technology agreement before anything gets bought. I'd probably go on one of their courses if the company paid and it was in work time, but I'm not doing night classes on computers at 43. At home we'd keep a bit more in savings, maybe stop the second holiday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's like hearing a creak in a pole you've just climbed. Probably fine, but you don't forget it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd go on a course only if the company paid. What if they didn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I wouldn't, and I'd argue they should. If they want us to learn their systems, that's their cost, not mine. My dad's lot at the steelworks got retraining money in the eighties only because the union fought for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the crew would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Ray. He's fifty-six and he's never sent an email in his life, worse than me. He'd be the first one they'd try to push out with a nice-sounding early retirement deal.

S1.say: We need a union technology agreement in writing before they buy anything. Drones and planning software are fine as long as nobody loses their job because of them.
S1.think: It worries me more than I show, because the drone trial out past Kettle Farm already does part of our inspection walks. If they need fewer of us, an average lineworker like me isn't safe.
S1.do: Pushes the branch for a technology agreement before any purchases and goes on company training only if it's paid and in work hours. Keeps more in savings and drops the family's second holiday.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a creak in a pole he's just climbed.
S1.quote: If they want us to learn their systems, that's their cost, not mine.
S1.fieldNote: His instinct is to protect the job through the union rather than change himself. He admitted he's average at the work, which sharpened his worry. He worries for an older colleague who is even less at home with computers than he is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need the government to step in, now, not after. Freeze the layoffs, tax the companies that replace people, keep the grid in public hands. I'd be at every rally they called.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, two years is nothing. I'm 43 with a mortgage and two kids, and I've got one trade. If a robot can climb a pole and splice a line in the rain, the company will buy it the minute it's cheaper than me, and the shareholders will cheer. Three months of savings doesn't get you far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd sit down with Mira and cut everything we could, the car upgrade, Sam's football camp maybe, the takeaway Fridays. I'd go straight to the union and get involved properly, and I'd ring the bank about the mortgage before they ring me. If I got laid off, I'd lean on whatever help there was, and Mira's wage, and I'm not ashamed of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, to be honest. Like a phone call at night when you know before you pick up that it's bad news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years of warning, what would you try to do before it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not a lot, that's what scares me. You can't learn a new trade in two years while working full time and doing call-outs, and anyway, what trade? I'd just try to pay off a bit more mortgage and hold on to the job as long as the union could keep me there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ellie and Sam?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the truth, that dad might lose his job, but it's not because he did anything wrong. Ellie would want to know if we'd lose the house. I'd say not if I can help it, but I wouldn't promise her.

S2.say: The government has to step in now: freeze layoffs, tax companies that replace workers and keep the grid public. He'd be at every rally.
S2.think: Two years is nothing for a 43-year-old with one trade, a mortgage and three months of savings. The company would buy the robot as soon as it's cheaper than him.
S2.do: Cuts household spending straight away, including the car upgrade and takeaway Fridays, and gets properly involved in the union. Calls the bank about the mortgage early and would lean on public help and Mira's wage if laid off.
S2.feel: Sick, like a late-night phone call he knows is bad news.
S2.quote: You can't learn a new trade in two years while working full time and doing call-outs, and anyway, what trade?
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture hit him hard because he sees no route out of his trade in two years. He blames shareholders and wants government and union action. He was honest that he wouldn't promise his daughter they'd keep the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, but louder. I'd say we've got five years to get proper protections in place, and if the politicians waste them, that's on them. I'd be telling everyone at the depot to join the union if they haven't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is better than two, I won't lie. Ellie would be seventeen, Sam fourteen, and we'd have a few more years off the mortgage. But I'd still be 48 and out of work in a town where the only other jobs are warehouses, and they'll have robots too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder, try to get to six months put by instead of three, and overpay the mortgage a bit. I'd put my name forward for the branch committee and write to our local politicians. Maybe I'd look at getting my heavy truck licence, but if robots do everything, trucks go too, so I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not as bad as the two-year one, but it'd sit on my chest every day for five years, which is its own kind of tiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years actually change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mainly the money and the kids' ages. With five years we could get the savings up and maybe Mira could pick up more shifts. It doesn't change the end, though. It just means I see the wave coming instead of it hitting me from behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd look at a heavy truck licence, then said that goes too. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point, I'm going round in circles. I think I'd look at it because doing something feels better than nothing. But really I'd be betting on the union and the government, not on me finding a new trade.

S3.say: There are five years to put proper protections in place, and if politicians waste them it's on them. He'd urge everyone at the depot to join the union.
S3.think: Five years helps with the mortgage and the kids' ages, but he'd still be 48 with one trade in a town where the other jobs are warehouses that robots will run too. The extra time changes the run-up, not the end.
S3.do: Saves hard to get from three to six months of savings and overpays the mortgage. Stands for the union branch committee and writes to local politicians, and half-considers a heavy truck licence.
S3.feel: Anxious, a weight on his chest every day for five years.
S3.quote: It just means I see the wave coming instead of it hitting me from behind.
S3.fieldNote: Gareth admitted he was going in circles about retraining. In the end he's betting on collective protection, not on changing trade himself. The extra time eased the money worry but not the deeper fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, so there's no excuse. Shorter hours, retraining money, a proper safety net, and the grid stays public. I'd want the union pushing for all of it from day one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is the one where I can almost picture being alright. I'd be 53, the kids would be grown, and the mortgage would be down to the last few years. I'm still not going to become some computer person, though. I'd be hoping to hang on till near the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on working and save steadily, nothing dramatic. I'd stay active in the union and vote for whoever has a real plan for workers. Mostly I'd wait and see how it goes in the first few years before I'd change anything big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can breathe. It's like knowing your knees will go one day. You don't like it, but you can plan around it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you've got a decade, why wait and see rather than start now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen a lot of big predictions come to nothing, like I said with the hype one. If I tear up my life on a forecast and it's wrong, I've lost a good job for nothing. I'd rather keep my head down and move when it's clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you hope Ellie and Sam do with that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ellie wants to be a vet, and I'd tell her to go for it, because you'd want a person with your dog. Sam's nine and wants to be a footballer, so we'll see. I'd just want them in a job where people still count.

S4.say: Ten years is enough to do this properly, so there's no excuse: shorter hours, retraining money, a real safety net and a public grid. The union should push for it all from day one.
S4.think: Ten years is the version where he can almost picture being alright, at 53 with grown kids and most of the mortgage paid. He still won't become a computer person and hopes to hang on near the end.
S4.do: Keeps working and saves steadily without big changes. Stays active in the union, votes for a party with a plan for workers and waits a few years before making any major move.
S4.feel: Uneasy but able to breathe, like knowing his knees will go one day.
S4.quote: If I tear up my life on a forecast and it's wrong, I've lost a good job for nothing.
S4.fieldNote: The long runway turns his resistance into a reasoned waiting game. His mood eased mostly because of his life stage: grown kids and a smaller mortgage by 2036. He wants his children in work where people still count.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. What would help is a deal that keeps people like me in work while things change, or proper money if they don't, enough to keep the house. And retraining in work time, paid, not a website you're meant to do at night.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who gets the money. If a robot does my job for less, someone's pocketing the difference. I'd want some of that going back to the people it replaced, and to towns like ours, not just to head office.

headlineQuote: If a robot does my job for less, someone's pocketing the difference.
portrait: Gareth Varga is a 43-year-old lineworker out of a rural depot, nineteen years in, a union man like his father, with a nurse partner, two kids and fourteen years left on the mortgage. He doesn't use AI tools and is proud of it, and he judges every new system by whether it ever reaches the bucket truck. The calm picture relieves him, the steady one makes him push for a union technology deal, and the fast AGI picture leaves him sick with worry because he sees no other trade to move to. More warning time eases the money worry, but his plan stays the same: lean on the union and the government rather than reinvent himself.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because two years is too short to change trade with a mortgage, two kids and three months of savings.
whatWouldHelp: A deal that keeps workers in their jobs during the change, or real income support enough to keep the house, plus paid retraining in work time. He also wants the savings from robots shared with the people and towns they replace.
